So let's talk about Kant. Emanuel Kant was the greatest philosopher who ever lived because he introduced us to the idea that we are not observers of reality, but participants in it. The nana, which means reality outside of us or things in themselves, is something we can never truly know because whenever we perceive reality, we filter it through time and space. Time and space do not exist outside of us; they are part of our perception, allowing us to make sense of the world.

This creates three problems: first, what exactly is the nana? Second, why do we have these filters of time and space? And third, how can we ensure that what I see is the same as what you see if reality is a subjective experience? Hegel came along and explained the idea of the gist. He suggested that the nana is really the spirit world or gist, which gives us our perception of time and space. Because everything comes from this one source, we all perceive the world in the same way.

Moving on to quantum mechanics, in science class, you're taught the neo-bore model of the atom, a simple model with a nucleus and orbiting electrons. But if you study more advanced physics, you learn that atoms are not solid matter but vibrations or quantum fields. Electrons are intersections of these fields, which can exist as both waves and particles depending on observation, a phenomenon known as wave function collapse.

Physicist Erwin Schrödinger created the thought experiment called Schrödinger's cat to illustrate this concept. In an unopened box, the cat is both dead and alive until observed. This demonstrates that before interaction, reality exists in multiple states simultaneously.

Another physicist introduced the friend experiment or Wigner's friend, further exploring these ideas of quantum superposition and observer influence on reality.
